chunks: "I start from the requirements, because the datasheet is only useful once I know what I'm comparing against. I'd ask: what is the input range, including transients and hot-plug?
What output voltage and how much current, continuous and peak? What are ripple, noise and transient limits? Is it battery powered, so quiescent current matters?
How much board area, what ambient temperature, any EMI limits?. Then I filter. Voltage rating: I want V IN(max) with margin, because ringing can double the input.
Current: the IC's continuous rating should be well above my load, and I check the current limit.
Duty cycle: I compute V OUT over V IN at both ends and make sure the on-time at my chosen frequency is longer than the part's minimum on-time.
Then efficiency and thermals: I estimate losses at full load, multiply by theta JA and check junction temperature at max ambient.
After that come the softer things: control mode and light-load efficiency, switching frequency versus passive size and EMI, integrated or external compensation, protections, package and cost.
I'd shortlist two or three parts, build a quick loss and ripple estimate in a spreadsheet, and validate the pick on a real board."
